entries.t: Cannabis Domesticated ~12,000 Years Ago in East Asia
entries.b: Whole-genome resequencing of 110 global cannabis accessions proved a single domestication event in early Neolithic East Asia, ~12,000 years ago. All fiber-hemp and drug-type cultivars share one ancestor, with the fiber/drug split occurring ~4,000 years ago through targeted gene selection.
entries.src: Ren et al., Science Advances 7(29): eabg2286 (2021)
entries.extract: C. sativa was first domesticated in early Neolithic times in East Asia, ~12,000 years ago, and all current hemp and drug cultivars diverged from an ancestral gene pool still represented by feral plants in China.

entries.t: Ritual Cannabis Smoking in the Pamir Mountains, 500 BCE
entries.b: GC-MS analysis of ten wooden braziers from Jirzankal Cemetery (eastern Pamirs, ~500 BCE) detected cannabinol (CBN) — the combustion product of THC — in nine braziers and on heated stones. The elevated CBN signal exceeded modern wild cannabis, implying selection for potent plants for funerary inhalation rituals at 3,000 m altitude.
entries.src: Ren et al., Science Advances 5(6): eaaw1391 (2019)
entries.extract: Chemical residue evidence from the first millennium BCE in the Pamirs: earliest directly dated, scientifically verified evidence of ritual cannabis smoking.

image.caption: Pamir Plateau, Xinjiang — site of the Jirzankal Cemetery where 2,500-year-old wooden braziers tested positive for cannabinol via GC-MS

entries.t: The Yanghai Shaman's Stash: 789g of Ancient Cannabis, ~700 BCE
entries.b: A 2,700-year-old shaman's tomb at Yanghai, Turpan Basin, Xinjiang yielded 789 grams of cannabis packed in a wooden bowl — female flowering tops, no fiber goods present. Phytochemical and genetic analyses confirmed psychoactive drug-type cannabis, preserved by extreme desert aridity.
entries.src: Russo et al., Journal of Experimental Botany 59(15): 4171–4182 (2008)
entries.extract: Yanghai tomb M90 contained the world's oldest confirmed cannabis psychoactive cache: 789g of female inflorescences with a shamanistic burial context.

entries.t: Cannabis Burial Shroud at Jiayi Cemetery, ~2,500 BP
entries.b: Thirteen complete Cannabis sativa plants, dated 2,800–2,400 years old, were found laid as a burial shroud over a 35-year-old man in Jiayi Cemetery, Turpan. Flowering tops bore intact glandular trichomes indicating drug-type cannabis; no fiber use was identified — the first whole-plant cannabis find from any ancient site.

entries.t: Cannabis on Iron Age Israelite Altars, Tel Arad, ~760–715 BCE
entries.b: GC-MS residue analysis of two limestone altars from Tel Arad's Iron Age shrine (Beer-sheba Valley, Israel) detected THC, CBD, CBN, and cannabis terpenes on the smaller altar, burned in animal dung. The frankincense-and-cannabis pairing suggests deliberate psychopharmacological ritual — the earliest cannabis evidence in the Ancient Near East.

image.caption: Tel Arad Israelite shrine (Iron Age, ~760–715 BCE), where GC-MS analysis of the altar surface revealed THC, CBD, and CBN residues

entries.t: Bronze Age Cannabis Seeds at Haimenkou, Yunnan, 1650–400 BCE
entries.b: Over 800 cannabis seeds from the waterlogged Bronze Age site of Haimenkou, Yunnan (1650–400 BCE) underwent morphometric analysis. Seeds fell between wild and domesticated types — cannabis caught in transition toward fiber or drug specialization, evidencing a regionally distinct SW Chinese domestication trajectory.
entries.src: Dal Martello et al., Vegetation History and Archaeobotany 33: 503–520 (2023)

entries.t: Cannabis as Core Crop: Phytolith Evidence from Shandong, 4,500–3,400 BP
entries.b: Phytolith analysis of 132 samples from two Shandong Neolithic settlements found cannabis in 68–72% of domestic contexts alongside millet and rice. Cannabis was not a marginal or ritual plant but a systematically cultivated staple crop deeply integrated into daily farming life 4,500 years ago — earlier than previously confirmed.
entries.src: Shandong University/CAS team, Journal of Archaeological Science (2026)

entries.b: Wageningen University researchers computationally reconstructed and synthesized ancestral cannabinoid synthase enzymes predating the cannabis/hops divergence, 25+ million years ago. These ancient enzymes were biochemical generalists producing THCA, CBDA, and CBCA simultaneously; modern specialized THCAS and CBDAS arose via gene duplication and a four-residue loop insertion.
entries.src: Villard, Baser et al., Plant Biotechnology Journal (2025), DOI: 10.1111/pbi.70475

facts.text: The world's oldest cannabis stash — 789g in a Yanghai shaman's wooden bowl, ~700 BCE — predates the founding of Rome by over 200 years and remains greentinged after 2,700 years of Gobi Desert preservation.
Cannabis and hops (Humulus lupulus, used in brewing) share an ancestral enzyme from >25 million years ago — before they diverged into separate genera. Beer and cannabis share deep biochemical roots.

The Jirzankal braziers at 3,000 m elevation showed CBN signals stronger than modern wild cannabis. High-altitude UV radiation increases THC biosynthesis — the Pamir mountains may have been a natural 'potency amplifier.'

At Tel Arad's 'holy of holies,' two altars were deliberately paired: one with cannabis (psychoactive), one with frankincense (which contains the anxiolytic incensole acetate) — a sophisticated 2,700-year-old guided-experience protocol.
Phytoliths are silica ghost-casts of plant cells. Cannabis phytoliths survived 4,500 years in Shandong agricultural soil where no seeds or fibers could have persisted — silica simply doesn't rot.

Every cannabis plant on Earth — from Oregon dispensaries to Indian charas to European hemp — traces to a single domestication event in Neolithic China ~12,000 years ago. One people, one place, one origin.

The 13 cannabis plants found as a burial shroud at Jiayi Cemetery, Turpan (2,500 BP) still had intact glandular trichomes — the microscopic structures that produce THC — visible under a microscope after 2,500 years in desert sand.

Shandong phytolith data found cannabis in >68% of domestic samples alongside millet and rice — suggesting cannabis was as ordinary and essential to Neolithic northern Chinese farmers as wheat is in a modern kitchen.

gallery.caption: Botanical plate of Cannabis sativa from Köhler's Medizinal-Pflanzen (1887), showing male/female anatomy and seed — the same plant domesticated in Neolithic East Asia ~12,000 years ago.

Tel Arad Israelite shrine, Beer-sheba Valley, Israel (~760–715 BCE). GC-MS of the smaller altar yielded THC, CBD, and CBN — the earliest cannabis evidence in the Ancient Near East (Arie et al., 2020).
Limestone altar from Tel Arad, Israel. Paired altars in the shrine's inner sanctum held cannabis and frankincense respectively — an intentional dual-drug ritual arrangement.

Living Cannabis sativa plant. All modern varieties are descendants of a single Neolithic domestication ~12,000 years ago in East Asia, confirmed by whole-genome resequencing of 110 global accessions (Ren et al., 2021).

Map of Xinjiang, China — home to Jirzankal (500 BCE braziers), Yanghai (2,700-year-old shaman's stash), and Jiayi (2,500-year-old cannabis burial shroud) — the richest region on Earth for ancient cannabis archaeology.

Woodcut of cannabis from Leonhart Fuchs's De Historia Stirpium (1542) — one of the first printed European botanical records, made as living oral traditions of cannabis use stretched unbroken from Neolithic Asia to the Renaissance.
